Let me tell you how national happiness was measured when I was a little girl. In the census you were asked whether you were married, white, and a homeowner; and if your answers were yes, your unhappiness was measured by how much of the time you were below the bottom tenth percentile of American income. If you answered no, the census didn't want anything from you. You were failures, and you were responsible for your failures, and you were ugly, and you would never be important persons.

Let me tell you how national happiness is measured now. It includes the prosperity of every person in the United States, rich or poor, hispanic or white: not just his income but his or her health, which is what being married to a doctor and owning a home used to mean; and education, which is what being white used to mean. Back then the United States was competitive with Denmark, Sweden, and Germany, the other countries historians used to call inhuman. Now it lags as a nation.

The different way of measuring changed what we could look at, and so it changed what we looked at, and so it changed what we knew, and so it changed our conversation. Our conversation used to be: domestic violence and child abuse are private family matters. Our conversation is: domestic violence and child abuse are loosely organized, largely state-organized crimes.

Our conversation used to be: to have children you must legally acquire the resources to parent them or be judged a bad person. Frank exhaled.

If $32,400 buys Nadia Haddad's place on Main Street for another five years, I want to be the family trust that makes it possible. I wrote a check for $400.

How much convenience is workable

Even by the most generous stretch of the imagination, driving a car is a huge waste of time. If you drive an hour to, say, work, you spend another hour coming home. Then, in your recreational hours, you may spend hours a week doing maintenance—ignition services, oil changes, visual inspections. This all adds up to a lot of time: In 2016, U.S. drivers logged some 3.2 trillion miles, or 6.4 million hours every day (that's 45 billion hours a year or almost 585 hours per household). About 1.3 trillion of those miles were for getting to and from regular destinations, a far cry from the “Sunday drive” vision they inspire. But even if we accept all this time spent driving, economists generally find that the middle class would have to be willing to accept an extra six-figure income in order to trade constant car readiness for constant car-free life. At what income level would this tradeoff be indifferent? “If Per Capita National Income Is Set at $99,000 and Households Travel 34 Min./Day,” a 1972 paper by Carl Adamson made famous by Alex Tabarrok found “the reconstructed indifference curve . . . queries at approximately 44 min.” So, 44 minutes a day is an acceptable amount of time to spend in the car.

Admittedly, this is not the purpose of Andy Singer’s TALK TO ME FRIDA (Farrar, 2023); it’s the incident that sets off the feedback loop.

My mother had been treasurer of our parents' investment club throughout my childhood. In the 1990s I initiated a fantasy investment-stock portfolio, and a few thousand dollars that had been set aside for my college education ended up going instead toward playing the market. For a while the balance would go up, and up, and up—I'd add an after-school job to the money I received as allowance, all of it deposited immediately into my brokerage account. Then it would go down, and down, and down—I'd have to shame my parents into giving me gifts of cash. I reached the $100,000 mark in 2003, a year after I graduated from college. My fund lost half its value that year. By 2009 it was below $10,000. I stopped logging in to the account.

There are locations where the tables have turned, my mother said, wistfully. In the 1920s someone made $5 million on a $100 investment, a commission on a single, illiquid bond issue. But that man died at seventeen with appendicitis, and now his family is living the same life as everyone else's.

On December 20, 2019, my parents received a letter from one of their regular correspondents, who I''ll never know. Maybe you don't want to hear from me anymore—I do get that. But I'm really throwing away something that might be fruitless.

Please just hear me out.

A mother is like a thug in a sense. I think we'd all agree that the best-case scenario is within the happy family, but thug mothers still have to buy cannolis on the way home from school.

I searched for a news report about the letter.

Three New Jersey children received letters last week from a "Elmo"-themed food interior, according to the AP.

Two of the children are New Jersey natives, and one, an eight-year-old girl, is from West Orange, N.J. She said that after receiving the letter, she immediately went to her parents' home to tell them the cat had died.

"We felt so terrible for him," the child said. "I don't think he had a chance."

A police spokesman said the letter had not been opened and had not been addressed to the child.

It had been addressed to him directly. He had personally renewed the postage on the envelope, left it in his fiancée's filing cabinet, and brought it back one last time before he left

Nadia was minutes from calling Frank, but first she sent the link to her husband, Shaheen, the father of their three sons.

I've got to sleep now. I'm waking him up tomorrow, she thought. I can't do it. I'm going to wake up dead.

She felt sick. She leaned over from the couch and vomited in the toilet. Her phone pinged.

She looked at the message from Shaheen: You did it!!

He had donated $25 to catch her up to the homeless guy. Fear honored her with a peace so perfect it was unearthly, and she laughed until she cried. Frank called to tell her the good news.

Paul Magnum

Friend of Paul's, first, I want you to know how wonderful it is to feel interesting again. I'd lost touch with my self-worth and didn't see why enjoying or appreciating things should be any kind of priority for me. Pardo questioned some of that. I thought it was enough to wake up in a safe bed every day.

But I'm most grateful, friend of Paul's, for the sense of mystery you introduced me to. I haven't chased it so much as it's crept in unnoticed. There's something inched its way through the safeguards and walls, and I almost welcome it at this point. I'm fascinated. I understand a little, but putting my finger on it doesn't change the essential truth, which is that I don't know. Not so that would cover it.

You reminded me, friend of Paul's, of an essay by Lithub's editor Ian Frazier called the "Slump Buster." He opens it with an anecdote about an old woman who, upon waking up in bed each day, rued the fact she forgot the "answer" in her sleep. She'd nearly reached it the night before, but couldn't quite remember how it connected. She was deeply disappointed, and when the doctor, alarmed, asked her what her answer was, she replied: "If I had it I wouldn't have to wake up every morning."

Now that's depression.

But get this, friend of Paul, the wonderful thing here isn't that I'd gotten so wrapped up in stubborn facts, I'd forgotten the central truth that our existences are mysterious. The wonderful thing is that I'd almost given it up as hopeless. I was sharing that feeling of helplessness with that wonderful woman Frazier wrote about.

The next morning, Nadia, humming "We Are the Champions," pivoted through the front door, handing Frank a key to the bookstore's mailbox. "We named someone the hero of the town," she said. "He was the one who got the rest."

That the man who sold the prom queen in "Traffic Jam--Millbrook" was now milling the flour for the hero of the town was a fitting homecoming for Ron Buckwalter. It had been a homecoming for many, but none quite so orderly as his. He had returned in the spring of 2011, exactly twenty years after that Whalen girl pulled up the grass, after Jane Griswold told him to get out, after he hit that girl and really did ruin his sons. It had been exactly twenty years since he was sentenced. He began serving parole under supervision, and reluctantly he decided he needed something to keep him out of Donald's Halloween stash and out of his wayward daughters' modeling portfolios. He had avoided any of the kind of menial pursuits that put kitchen-table heroes off their meals. He had had his choice between Arby's full time in Millbrook and a location in nearby Balmville. He chose Millbrook, only for Adam Weiner’s approval.

Last Saturday afternoon the students of Chapter & Verse were at the front of the bookstore dressed as their favorite characters for literary costume contest. Nadia was wearing the sleeves from an old sweater that she'd embroidered into eyepatches and a scarf headband to look like Mal, from A Wrinkle in Time, and Cosette was at her side as Eponine, with a full-face tan. Nadia had revealed the winner—an eleventh-grade girl as Daisy Buchanan in The Great Gatsby—but as tradition dictated, the announcement was not to be made public for twenty-four hours. The crowd of kids was still milling, settling into chairs for movie night and flicking through copies of the campus newspaper.

When Nadia announced the winner to the kids, she promised that she would try to publish all of the literary zines that had been submitted. "We haven't had a single negative submission," she said, meaning that nobody had dropped out of the contest after reading the guidelines. And looking at the stack of bright-colored, glitter-streaked, tape-bound zines in front of her, she was looking forward to reading them. She wasn't sure if she could publish a hundred and fifty zines, but she was going to try. She opened her speech, as she always did, by saying that if kids didn't get enough books to read from the library or the bookstore, they should stop by her house, and she would give them some of the used books.

Then she stepped back from the podium so the kids could take it back.

The Beasts

Miro Haggan, an artist with CDW, a construction company in West Reliant, had painted a mural of a giant purple dinosaur on the brick wall of a closed Beasts Pizza on Route 86, across from Sausage King and the exit to Salem Road.

The mural was his gift to Wyfoord, where he'd spent his childhood. The only thing he had liked about Pomadon was Michele Duncan, the tomboy next door, who saved him from years of torment in his school's drama club. He left Beasts for her, and for another reason: his father had been a drunk who arrived at home late on Wednesdays and Thursdays with smashed knees and a filthy yellow stain on his shirt. He'd worn jeans to work at the factory and khakis on weekends, and his truck was caked with dried puke and spilled beer. Construction was a solid job, but he wanted a job that he could get out of, and a good one.

On a Tuesday in January, Miro called Wyfoord's town council. "I've got this old creative juices going—I haven't painted in ten years—and we've got this wall." With a little help from the town and CDW, the fee he would traditionally charge for the work, and a Beasts gift card, he intended to turn the wall into new Beasts Pizza's grand opening event. He loved Wyfoord, and he wanted to help clean it up.

From that week on bands began to show up after dark and play on the restaurant's empty concrete porch while Miro painted. Some of them played old songs, and people danced around two plastic tables under the awning. Some of them played new songs, and people gathered to watch them do it.

Every day the wall grew brighter. A green grass-henze background for the dinosaur, and then a purple pine forest. Trees with purple vegetation bloomed in full color across the back wall, and purple flowers crawled up from the bottom and shot sparks like fireworks. With five minutes to go before the Lehigh Valley Potters Association's annual opening exhibit closes tonight, Anne McClure estimates that about eighty-five of the hundred or so objets d'art created by the region's potter guild that crowds the front gallery of the Allentown Art Museum should be purchased by patrons looking for their annual doily, or their aunt's birthday present.

Anne calls her totemic, stylized crab variation a Yielding Crab, though she refers to most of the figurines in her idiosyncratic vessel-builder idiom as her "wallowing creatures."

"At the parties, I call them my thrashing creatures," she cracked. "You need to be careful which word you use when you're in a public venue."

Midwestern critics, then, beware.

Anne started potting thirty years ago, after acquiring an art teacher's extraterritorial gift set of clay as a gift from a colleague. She completed a class certificate, leveled up, and eventually even finished a night class in kiln firing and design at Philadelphia's Moore College of Art and Design. You'd be shocked by how much Anne separates her personal and professional lives, she said, pointing to the latest of her five exes just now approaching her corner.

"I'll always treat them with love and respect," she said, but as Anne continues in potting even to this day, she'll leave recklessness and recreancy for them.

Today, almost all Americans are the secular descendants of Christians, and most of us don't care much about what happens to the Episcopal Church. But a century or so ago Episcopal religion functioned in much the same way that medicine, philosophy, and cosmology do today. It served the powerful and influential by providing them with explanations and rationalizations for their social, political, and economic positions, and it served the less powerful by giving them beliefs to believe. It provided a community to its schools and hospitals and soup kitchens, and like those institutions it created and enforced a series of mental boundaries around what is and is not right to think and what to do and how to act, whether inside the church itself or outside it. Frank flipped some charcoal onto the ashtray, relighting the cigar he'd been smoking for the last three hours. No one had worked that hard, and earned that much, by folding when they were two hundred dollars short of a deal.

He opened his email. "Baby," his daughter Theresa wrote, "I talked to my Uncle Phil and he finally said he would help you. Attached is the check. Let me know once you've gotten it. Love you, Theresa."

The attachment showed a check made out to Frank for $645, drawn on a Southwest Florida bank. Frank hit Reply and forwarded the email, with the check attached, to the crowdfunding page. He turned off his tablet, his phone, and his computer and went to bed.

At noon on Saturday Nadia called: "Guess what happened?"

"What did it say on the check?"

"Dear Henry. Love Bobby."

"Thank him for me. And IT guy?"

"Adjustments took about forty minutes. It bounced."

"They made some modifications to my check, sent it through twice. My name was cleaned up and all the date fields were right. And the signature was good." Frank shook his head. "We met once, at Theresa's graduation from Fordham. He gave a speech."

"You said nobody named Bobby Foreman was on the Southwest Florida shareholders list. Who else could it be?"

"Nad. Don't. Don't you ever."

"But you figured it out."

"They closed down the First National Bank of Palm Beach three months ago after they found out the Second National Bank of Coral Gables was a front. Five years in the slammer."

"And they never printed another check. Who knows if there's another holder out there?"

"Don't even make fun of what I did."

"It's like a story by the Master Danda, the Nigerian kind."

"Had to."

"I'm sorry."

"Yeah. Play me."

"What should I write? 'Dear Frank, Please accept this allowance check from your daughter. It covers our rent for the next year? Best, Bobby.'"

"I'm not going to tell her."

"You're plotting a kinder version of Massacre at Silvanus Cole's Funeral."

"A little."

"I love you."

"Probably a mistake." Frank hung up. He burned unsmoked cigars in the backyard and paid a kid from down the street five bucks to wear his Notre Dame sweat suit into town and mail the check to Theresa's address.

Frank put his face in his hands and felt like crying.

Then suddenly he felt something new. It was a strong feeling, almost like an emotion, pulsing through his chest and his arms and his neck. It was hard to name, but whatever it was, he hadn't felt it in thirty-one years. What the hell? Had he just had a blip of something he could use to . . . do good?

Then the numbers on his tablet began to roll over, like grains of sand falling through an hourglass. At 12:00 the total came up as $32,001, eight hundred and one dollars in donations in the last sixty seconds of the campaign. And then it kept rising. By 12:03 it stood at $33,319, good for drinks for all those Belleville hard cases a couple of days ago.

At 12:19 it stood at $39,322, and Frank decided he would let the campaign stay open indefinitely. It wasn't the money that changed him, of course, not really. Anyone who thinks the material purchase of a used Audi or a season's tickets to the Cleveland Cubs automatically fulfills a life-long dream is kidding themselves. It wasn't the money, per se.

Nor was it pity for a small indie bookstore struggling to survive in a retail business that looked more and more doomed by the day; Chapter & Verse was too profitable through too many years of the Great Recession for Frank to buy that. Three months ago Nadia had bought a second rental unit in Chagrin Falls for $56,000, no down payment.

So what changed him? Nadia came to the door at after three o'clock on Saturday. She wasn't crying, as he'd somehow expected she might be, but her eyes were red and puffy. She hugged him, carefully enough not to break his ribs. He squeezed her a little back. He had no idea what to say.

Then she said it: "You are my hero."

That's when it really hit him. He'd had people describe him as a hero, people who actually knew him. He hadn't had that since spring tour '67, when he caught Max Webster after he got too close to that revolving door on Euclid Avenue, keeping him from losing a finger. People had thanked him personally, and the next day one of the papers ran a big picture of him in jeans and a linen blazer holding the door.

The Ithaca Landlords Association met on the first Tuesday of every other month. Attendees moved directly from the just-before-room to the just-after-room at the Hilton, approximately the same size as a shoebox. A coffee mug with Russian lettering and a set of coasters distinguished the one room from the other. Most of the landlords were landlady-lawyers or building managers and came into the Ithaca area on the train every month from Elmira or Rochester.

The rental market in Ithaca was relatively safe, by this time in the rent-unabated-inflation cycle: vacancy rates were two and a half percent, rents had risen four and a half percent the previous year, singly-family homes $25,000 on average. The level of the market hadn't risen to the point where there were pushouts or evictions. What gathered these men and women together that day, the subject for which they were paying $100 each to discuss, was a phenomenon that was only beginning and, for the moment, affected relatively few units: the crowdfunded rent gap.

Some of it was one-time affairs like what had happened in Millbrook. Those always resolved themselves one way or another, depending on the kindness or sensibility of the landlord. But there was real trouble in the form of Get-an-Apartment-online and Launchalife. Frank was disappointed. He was also furious at himself. He'd been staring at the site for nearly six hours, watching the goal inch upward. If he'd clicked the button $20 had come up with the rest. He stared at the page. It took a few moments to sink in.

The donors of Millbrook had saved Nadia Haddad, whose business had started during the pandemic and which, like many independent bookstores, never really left home. They had saved her bookshelves and the bear rug beside which she napped, the "Hot Dog Door," the writer Eliza Mueller, and her family, who cared for ducks, hens, and Stella the retired racing greyhound. And they had saved Frank Kowalski, who, even if he felt no better about it, could now afford to leave the town he had moved to from Brooklyn two and a half decades ago.

He inserted his debit card into the machine by his sink—and took it out again. It shouldn't be his money. But why should it be anyone else's this time? They'd given her enough. His mind snagged. Frank remembered the to-do list he'd set on his calendar years earlier, when Irene's dementia had been progressing and the direction in which it was headed had become clear: home care (if verified medically necessary), nursing home, assisted living, and memory care—and if medical science hadn't caught up in twelve years, hospice (their home, theirs).

That had taken money he'd never had. If you live in America and don't want to starve to death, you have to save money: for college, for postcollegiate training, for trade tools, for retirement. The cost of having children means the normal person can't have more than two and rarely more than one, and maybe not even one, since even young people priced out of high rents racket up student loans paying tuition and LIVING EXPENSES so big they could buy houses—or maybe they just don't want to.

People, all over the country, save. Or they used to. But savings take time to accumulate, and time goes funny, these days. In the time it took Frank to go from pleasantly retired senior citizen to horrified caregiver, Americans ran out of money. He was moving his wife to memory care, he had to have a cot in her room, and he had nothing that he could wear on his nights there.

Frank felt a weight lift from his chest as he stood and folded up his tablet. It was the weight of her, lying so insubstantial even on the air in any room she hadn't been in for years. It had grown almost indistinguishable from his own these days; he couldn't tell if it was hers or his that had used up all the air.

Irene slid into memory care the way pond scum slides into the water. He had not seen the change coming, and suddenly she was tucked into the miniature recreation of a suburban life. Technically she still owned half of the building, but she had taken to handing over everything anyone asked for, including her role on the deed. Maybe it was how Ikowski urged Frank to let go, tell her at least the terms of the deal—the chain's rent, the accelerated deadline she'd have to meet, her renewal if she beat it. And he did. But he kept his voice low and didn't look at her as he spoke. Maybe if she hadn't been suffering so many small losses already, she would have heard him. Maybe if he were a cruder man, he could have expressed himself in a more crude way. Maybe if he had kept talking, she would have started (again) to fall back in time, all the way. If he had said this to her, for instance: why were you nice when I was mean, why were you starving when I was enjoying my food? How are we each other, how are we married, what are you doing here?

Frank bought groceries and drove his truck to the VIN Etching Business on Abrams Road to get his windshield repaired. An older Latino man with short hair was fixing the windshield of another truck outside.

"Pull in home right," the man called to Frank, who had backed into a space in front. "If you fit, I fit 'cha. Same window."

Frank swung his cab to the left and eased in without hitting the cars on either side.

"Hold on a minute. Hot out, huh?" The man, Armando, walked over.

"The girls are hot, huh?" They laughed. "Move that truck up two feet."

Frank handed him his ID via the open window while Armando worked on the windshield position. "So what brings you back to the block?" The question made Frank consider the irony of his predicament.

"Never left," he said, thinking he always knew what his near future would hold, and so did she. He winced at his own treachery. He had taken this business for granted over the years and he wasn't sure what gratitude even looked like anymore, what it meant to try and offer it. He was running out of time.

"Nah. Back again," Armando said. "I was a hobbie dyer. Couldn't take my blade out of my blood no more." He pointed to the first and third knuckles of his left hand.

Oscar Hammerstein II had got on the wrong side of Mayer and Thalberg at Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer during the writing of the script for "The Wizard of Oz." There was never a chance for a second draft. His worst instincts had been given free rein. The script had been produced almost exactly as written, by people who didn't give a damn about it. On the opening day, a room full of people waited for his verdict.

"How did I like it?" He hesitated. He couldn't save face after bemoaning the casting. "The score is wonderful," he said. "Schönberg wrote it." Schönberg had written it, hadn't he? The score was wondrous. "But it's too sad." He wasn't talking about the Sad Man—only his agent ever did that. "Too sad for children."

Instead of eating the glares in the room, Hammerstein ran to the bathroom and stood up on the toilet, bracing first one foot and then the other against the edge of the sink. He lowered himself to the floor and stepped off the toilet.

The next day Frank went to Millbrook's town hall to sign Nadia's lease. After she had left with photocopies, a young woman named Tasha Freitag approached him. Tasha was twenty-nine, zero pounds overweight, with two narrow braids and a stonewashed sleeveless sweatshirt. "I'm familiar with this place," she said, and Frank figured she was another child's childhood bedtime story. "Most of the profits from my book, in paperback, go to the UCSF Neuroendocrine Tumor Research Foundation, and I've read that you guys host readings here. A bookstore with a readings series, I have to stop in, and—"

"I respect that you want to contribute," he said, "but I have to charge you."

Tasha had arranged an event with a local poet called the Prop and the Paint for March. Her book would be for sale on 5×8 cards in a book-lined tiered box with three holes in it, and the props and paints would be cups of paint and brushes and wooden tomato stakes. People would write on the wooden stakes and then plant them in a patch of dirt by the front door, and Tasha would post a picture of each one the event's Facebook page. "My Facebook reach is small but mighty," she said.

"How much would you like for a slot that long?" Frank said.

Tasha calculated it in her head. "Eighteen a minute?" she said. "That works. I'd be happy to do that. I'll get a bite to eat up the street from here. I'm hungry anyway."

It was Friday, and the Book Group had already gathered in a circle of two rows of folding chairs. Eight regulars had crammed in, three others on the waiting list were spread about on the edges of the group. A puppet fifty-something led the night's discussion with a reading list in hand, and Nadia's assistant hovered behind them, like a consult for every word. Nadia herself was reading at the other side of the building, a show-and-tell about her car's electrical system.

Tasha arrived midway through the meeting and began to set up her props. She drove half the time with the steering wheel on her knees, fingers dancing across the threads of the seat belt. When the rotation of the road ran her down, it lifted her back up when her hands ran lightly down the seat belt, calming her nerves enough to bring her up.

The town had named a busy intersection Will Hart Drive after Joe's son. Frank had wanted to call it Cook College Circle, let people know what was in the college district, but it wasn't his intersection. He put his phone to his ear, but Jim didn't speak for almost a minute, and the longer it went on, the hotter and stickier his feet felt. Finally Jim said, "Congratulations."

The words made a picture in Frank's head of three chess pieces moving to make a threat, a sacrifice, but Frank didn't know who was threatened or where. "What'd they end up giving you?"

"They gave us $32,864," Jim said. "Dalton, Tom, and Nick live in Medford, and they stopped in this morning when they were going to work. They were glad to be there."

"Their store's on the way," Jim said.

"You know, Jim," Kowalski said. He had a long moustache and chest hair, thick and dark, white at the ends. Jim wished he were growing his little beard out, but he had a breakfast meeting, and a dog on a leash might not reassure the Gingrich girl, such a delicate little girl.

"That was the first thing I heard on the radio this afternoon, Jim."

"Thanks, Frank."

"Long time. Reminds me of how long Nadia's been there."

"Not that long, actually."

"Come visit us. The books we had in Mindfield are still here, and more from Mindfield's come in every day. It's not the greatest, but I'm not making that kind of money." Frank hung up and clicked off his radio. He tightened his hands against the pressure in his legs, the burning fatigue. Cigarettes and a beer, a bottle of cheap chablis, a piece of pizza with roasted garlic and gorgonzola. Some of the old stuff, a crossword after dinner, and he could feel good for about an hour and a half, the way he used to feel eight hours after a hard day's work, if the day's work hadn't been way more than eight hours. He turned the tablet over and set it on the table. He put his hands, one on top of the other, on top of the tablet.

Even after the relief came, it wasn't enough.

The signs sped by, Millbrook,latitude 42.234902, longitude -73.137160, then Exit 22, then Bear Mountain, and before he knew it he was parking behind the locked gate at the old depot. He sat in his car with his hands gripping the steering wheel and his eyes closed, breathing.

At length he got out. He touched the cold metal of the railings as he walked along the platform. The parking lot lights cast long, wavering shadows. He thought about Nadia, nineteen when she'd started the store, how she'd carpeted the floor with folding chairs and gotten her first credit card reader, then her first telephone line, her first real bank account. He couldn't see her face but she was smiling, he knew that much.

He took out his phone and turned on the flashlight. There was a key hidden under one of the floorplanks inside the waiting room. His fingers found it by memory.

Inside it smelled the way it always had, of old paper and new hopes. He turned on his phone's light and panned it across the empty shelves and the signboard with the holes where mystery and thriller had once been nailed up. His throat hurt. He drove slowly under the stars to the bookstore and let himself in through the back door. With a small flashlight he searched the small apartment upstairs. Empty. He ran the vacuum over the carpet to pretend he'd been there all day, and then he shut off the music he'd left playing, to give the appearance of having been there until a reasonable hour. Her phone went to voicemail.

"Hey, Nadia," he said. "It's Frank. It didn't come through, and I don't want to make a big deal about it, but I'm going to have to go with the mattress chain. I talked to the owner this morning. They're going ahead and sending a crew in on Monday. You might want to start boxing things up. Anyway, I hope you understand. You're a good tenant and I appreciate how you've kept the place up, and I'm really sorry it has to end this way."

He had learned to accept the shine of tears at the corners of his eyes. Some of the people who'd given big amounts had gathered their friends in person and sent them over to the bookstore with cash. Nadia was probably in the parking lot accepting handfuls of twenties through the door. She'd done something similar in high school, collecting pledges for a field trip to Washington, D.C., and he thought of her at sixteen, standing under the marquees of the closed movie houses on Main Street, counting money in the brisk July dusk.

He sat back in his chair and wept, his face wet against the cool metal of the tablet. When he looked up his eyes fell on a cookbook he'd bought when Irene moved in, Before the Calcium Drops. He opened it to a recipe for turkey tetrazzini and read it carefully, then closed the book and went to bed, smiling.

In the morning he called the mattress chain and cancelled their lease. When he called Nadia to tell her he'd done it, she sounded like she'd been crying.

"That was more money than I needed," he said.

"You should have let me know," she said.

"I did," he said. "Actually, I did."

When he opened his inbox in the morning, there was no message from Nadia. He was getting ready for work at two when he received the following email, the subject line of which was "loe 39 Main Street."

Dear Mr. Kowalski,

I don't know if you know this about me, but I almost never capitulate. I've had some victories, but what's more common is that I carry on for far too long when the sensible thing would have been to quit. I was that child who hated to lose at games and would rather keep playing than abandon the hopeless cause. I still feel that way about some things, but not about others. I've learned to pick my battles.

I am also stubborn in another way: about arithmetic. I'm a whiz at math. Numbers are my true love language, and when numbers tell me something, I listen.

A lot of towns have a Main Street that loops around to itself, but in Millbrook it's an actual circle. Once on a run I started at the post office on the south side and ran counterclockwise, all the way around the circle and back to the post office. It was an amazing feeling, returning to the exact spot I'd started from, the route mapped in my mind and body.

There are fourteen addresses on our circle, and we're number 39 but actually at number 1. Our tenant in #39 is directly across the street from the tenant in #1 and from #14, although #1 is The Useful Hardware and #14 is Millbrook Antiques. The addresses are arranged like the hours on a clock, and I have at various times thought of ours as 12 and everyone else's as numbers leading up to us.

But this morning I realized that if you start at #14 and go clockwise around the circle, we're number 39. I know it's nonsense, that there's no such thing as #39 Main Street. But the truth is, there is: it's the same as #1. I hope you'll accept the rent in that spirit. My campaign raised what you needed and a little extra, and we'll be signing a lease as soon as you're ready.

I love Millbrook and I love your building, and I'm proud to have Chapter & Verse in a space that's been home to so many other wonderful businesses. We're going to be here for a long time.

With gratitude

When he wasn't working at the bookstore, Nadia volunteered at the senior center, where she ran a writing workshop for Irene every other Wednesday. They arrived just as the clock struck midnight. The center was tucked into a restored church. Half the participants, women in their seventies and eighties, looked frail, but today Frank didn't realize them at first. He was looking for Nadia.

The room was small and bright, the air heavy with the late-spring humidity. The walls were painted a gentle color that almost passed for white, and the windows had been left uncovered, so the sun streamed in, lighting the faces of the women who sat in mismatched chairs, facing the front. In a line of metal stools behind the line of chairs stood half a dozen men, each holding a walker, some asleep, some chatting with one another.

Frank had the impression it was morning, but he had stopped to pick up donuts. He took out first his wedding ring, then the cell phone, then the wallet. At last he realized the room was not empty; it was full. He was in a state of shock, without any sense that his life - that Irene could ever be so gone. He had not seen her in two weeks, and now he was conscious for the very first time that she probably could have died without his being there, and she probably had died.

With some trepidation, he marked on the page one of the words that had rattled around in his brain during the days of waiting, his mind ricocheting in the narrow confines like a ball in a pinball machine.

It was a name that belonged to the past, but the past was never truly past, and the name had a gravity now, so he went ahead and added it.

Once he had marked the final word on the page, he saw he had written a letter, and he also saw that the letter's meaning was apparent to anyone who wished to look. He brought the sheet with him to the front desk, where the night nurse waited to check him in. She put on her mask and she pulled on her gloves.

The next day, Saturday, Father Michael walked into Chapter & Verse and found Nadia beaming. 

"Good morning, Father," she said. "I must show you! Frank Kowalski signed the lease. Five years."

"That is wonderful news, Nadia." Father Michael smiled, delighted for her. Chapter & Verse wasn't just a store; it was a community hub. "The town will be ecstatic."

Nadia paused, her smile dimming slightly. "It was close, Father. Too close. Frank... he needed the money. He's paying for his wife's care, and his property taxes went up. We almost lost the store to a mattress chain."

Father Michael felt a pang of sympathy for both of them. Frank building houses, Nadia building stories. He saw Frank most Sundays, always quiet in the back of the church. Both were pillars of the town, both doing what they could, and both in need of a little help.

"Well," he said, reaching for his wallet, "I'm glad we could all pitch in." He handed Nadia a $100 bill. "Consider it a donation to the continued spiritual enrichment of Millbrook."

Nadia laughed, accepting the money. "You always know how to make me smile, Father. But honestly, it wasn't just the big donations. It was everyone. Mrs. Henderson brought in a box of her late husband's first editions to sell. Old Man Hemlock, who hasn't spoken a word in years, wrote a check for fifty dollars. It was... powerful."

Father Michael nodded, and together they looked around the shop, at the warm glow of the lamps, the overflowing shelves, the scent of old paper and fresh ink. Chapter & Verse was more than books. It was a testament to the power of community, to the quiet ways people helped each other, and to the belief that even in the face of hardship, stories could—and would—prevail.

Frank closed his eyes. A wave of guilt washed over him. He did not send a text to Nadia. Instead, he called a real estate agent and told him to begin preparing the contract for the mattress chain.

Frank was a man who had spent his life measuring things in dollars and cents. In his mind, a debt of gratitude was not a matter of emotion, but a contractual obligation.

A week later Nadia learned that he had gone ahead with the other offer. She sent him a letter that read, in part: "I never thought you’d do this. I thought Chapter & Verse was more than just a number to you."

Frank didn't answer at first, but a week after that, he found himself driving to the bookstore. He went in, saw Nadia, and simply said, "I need to explain."

He told her about Irene, the taxes, the dwindling savings. He told her about measuring everything in dollars and cents. And then he said, "I know it doesn’t excuse what I did."

Nadia listened quietly, her expression unreadable. When he finished, she simply said, "I understand."

She paused, then added, "But understanding doesn't change what happened."

Frank nodded. "No, it doesn't."

He wanted to ask her to forgive him, but he couldn't bear the thought of adding another debt, even an emotional one, to the pile he already carried. He turned to leave.

At the door, Nadia said, "Frank?"

He turned back.

"Did you ever add up all the money I paid you over thirty-one years?"

Frank shook his head. He had never bothered.

"It’s a lot of money," Nadia said, "Enough to have made a difference."

Then she looked at him, her gaze steady and clear. "You could have told me."

Frank felt a wave of shame so profound it nearly buckled his knees. He hadn't thought of it that way. It had never occurred to him to ask for help.

He could see now that he had been calculating all along, but he had been calculating the wrong things. He had been counting dollars instead of kindness, debts instead of friendships. He had made a decision based on a ledger, but life was not a balance sheet.

He looked at Nadia, and for the first time in months, he felt truly, utterly lost

Frank leaned back in his chair, letting out a breath he didn't remember holding. He closed the page and grabbed his phone. He dialed Nadia's number. 

"Hi, Nadia," he said, once she answered. "I just saw the good news. Congratulations." The relief in his voice nearly choked him.

"Mr. Kowalski!" Nadia exclaimed, her voice bright with emotion. "We did it! We actually did it!"

"You did," Frank said, he wanted to say more, but couldn't find the words. "You and the whole town."

Nadia paused. "You know," she said quietly, "I'm sure you had other good reasons to want me to stay."

Frank was silent for a moment. He could tell her the truth. He could lay everything bare. But he couldn't. He wouldn't. "Of course," he said finally. "You're a good tenant, Nadia. And a vital part of the town."

"That's good to hear," Nadia said. "I guess I'll see you Monday to sign the new lease?"

"Monday it is," Frank said. "And Nadia?"

"Yes?"

"Thank you."

Frank hung up the phone. He sat at the kitchen table for a long time, staring at the empty space where the crowdfunding page had been. He tasted a guilty sweetness on his tongue. 

He knew he hadn't been entirely honest. But he also knew Irene would be well cared for, and Chapter & Verse would continue to be a haven for book lovers. And sometimes, Frank thought, that was all that mattered. 

---

**Note:** This story is the result of a prompt delivered for the writing club I attend. The source was a Real Life post on Reddit where someone's local bookstore was threatened by a rent increase. I spent some time thinking about the landlord's motivations, trying to portray him as a complex character rather than a simple villain. I made adjustments to the facts of the original post to fit my narrative.

Frank didn't know how to feel. He knew he was doing the right thing, but he couldn't help feeling a little angry. He had needed that money. He stared at the screen for a long time, then slowly closed the tablet.

His phone rang. It was Nadia.

“Frank,” she said, her voice thick with emotion. “We did it. We actually did it.”

“I saw,” he said, his voice flat.

“Oh, Frank, thank you. Thank you so much.”

“You’re welcome,” he said. “Five years.”

“Five years,” she repeated. “I don’t know how to ever repay you.”

“Just stay in Millbrook,” he said, then hung up the phone.

He sat there for a while, then walked upstairs and sat next to Irene. She was mostly asleep, her hands clasped in her lap. He took one of her hands in his, tracing the lines on her skin with his thumb. She stirred, and her eyes fluttered open.

“Frank?” she whispered.

“I’m here,” he said.

“Am I going to be okay?”

“You are, my love,” he said, even though he knew that wasn’t true.

He sat there for a long time, holding her hand. He didn’t tell her about the bookstore, about the money, about any of it. He just sat there, holding her hand, and tried to be thankful for the small things, even when they were hard.  He needed to figure out a way to care for her. And he had the feeling that he would. Maybe, just maybe, the town would help with that too.

---

Frank stood up and started to cry. He went out to the garage and pulled out a bottle of Suntory whisky and poured himself a glass, his hand shaking. He took a long drink, then another. After a while he walked back to the kitchen and sat down again.

He picked up the phone and called Nadia.

"Nadia," he said, his voice thick with emotion. "You did it."

"Frank?" Nadia's voice was barely a whisper. "We did it. We really did it."

"I'll see you Monday, and we'll sign the lease."

"Thank you, Frank," she said. "Thank you."

Frank hung up. He knew the dollar amount she had raised didn't tell the whole story. It wasn't just the money. It was all the people, the whole town, pulling together. She'd proven that someone cared, and it was a punch to the gut. The chain could have solved his problems, but it wouldn't have been honest. He filled his glass again and raised it in a silent toast: to honesty, to community, and to the woman who ran a bookstore and believed in them both.

He had a tough conversation with his wife, Irene, when she was lucid enough to understand. She cried, remembering all the books Frank had brought home to her over the years, reading them aloud over dinner. She knew what Chapter & Verse meant to the town. She told him he'd done the right thing. 

"A town without a bookstore," she said, her voice fading, "is a town without a soul."

Frank sat beside her and held her hand until she fell asleep. He was still worried about the future, but for tonight, he had a little peace. He still had Irene, and he still had Chapter & Verse. That was enough. For now, it was enough.

Sure, I'd be happy to help explain it to you. When you receive money that is considered a tax deduction, it means that you can reduce the amount of money you owe in taxes by the amount of the deduction. In this case, the tax deduction for the donations you received is up to thirty percent less than the amount sent. 

For example, if you received a donation of $100, you can reduce your taxes by $70 (which is thirty percent of $100). However, the value of the "To Kill a Mockingbird" gifts that Were sent to the donors as a token of appreciation is taxable. So if the gifts are worth $20 each, you would have to pay taxes on the $20, plus an additional $6 (which is thirty percent of $20).

To figure out the total amount of tax you would owe on the donations you received, you would need to add up the total amount of donations and subtract thirty percent from that amount. Then you would need to add the taxable value of the gifts. 

In this case, you received $36,000 in donations. Thirty percent of that is $10,800, so you can reduce your taxes by that amount. The taxable value of the gifts is $20 x 2 = $40. So your total tax liability for the donations is $10,800 + $40 = $10,84

Frank didn't want to lose her, so he made her an offer: if she could pay him the difference for the first year, $32,400, by midnight on Friday, he would sign her to a new five-year lease at her current rent. She said, “Call you back.” It meant she was running to get her phone. Seconds later she was laughing. “I want you to know it was a close call. Twenty dollars. One guy came through at the last minute. We're celebrating like crazy here with bagels and donuts.”

“I don't take ... I mean, I’m happy for you. Did it cover it?”

“We're at forty.”

"Not at all," he said. "You have enough to stay. Do you need anything else?"

"Me? No, not me. No, four zero."

He thought he might need to hear it again, but he knew that fifty was fifty. Fifty thousand dollars.

They hung up. He switched on the TV, flipped through his favorite shows, then turned it off again. The air was cool outside, and he put on slippers and a fleece pullover and went into his landscaped backyard. He'd spelled his and Irene's names in garden lights, which was a thing Irene had always said she'd love. The setting sun was trying to do them justice.
